title: 3 Bad Habits You Must Avoid This School Year https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2017/08/19/3-bad-habits-you-must-avoid-this-school-year/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Michael Linsin describes a predictable progression of bad habits — complacency, inconsistency, and resentment — that erodes a strong start to the school year within a matter of weeks. He explains that early-year enthusiasm and good behavior can lull teachers into complacency, which leads to small acts of inconsistency (ignoring a call-out, overlooking a sloppy transition), which in turn erodes student respect and provokes pushback, eventually producing frustration and resentment that damages the teacher-student relationship. Using a wildfire metaphor — complacency as kindling, inconsistency as the spark, resentment as the fire — Linsin frames the progression as extremely common but entirely avoidable through awareness and refusal to take even a single step down the 'slippery slope.' He closes with a direct call to action: recommit immediately to following the classroom management plan exactly as written.
points: A strong start to the school year commonly deteriorates through a predictable three-stage progression: complacency, inconsistency, and resentment.
Early-year student enthusiasm and good behavior can create a false sense of security that leads teachers to become complacent about enforcing standards.
Small acts of inconsistency — ignoring a call-out, overlooking a messy transition — erode student respect and prompt boundary-testing.
Unchecked, this progression produces genuine teacher resentment, which damages rapport, influence, and likability, and generates more misbehavior in turn.
The way to stop the progression is awareness of how quickly it happens, refusing to take even a single step down the slope, and recommitting to the plan exactly as written.
quotes: But then, three or four weeks in, things begin to change. Restlessness creeps in. Attitudes develop. Listening takes a nosedive and the room starts buzzing with voices and excitability.
The truth, however, is that slowly, imperceptibly, you’ve fallen into a progression of bad habits.
It can cause you to become complacent. It can cause you to let your guard down, take your foot off the gas, and question—in the far recesses of your mind—why you need to be such a stickler.
And slowly but surely, these small inconsistencies send the message to your new class that you don’t really mean what you say.
The end result is even more misbehavior, scant leverage to do much about it, and every day feeling like the Siege of Bastogne.
So right now, this second, vow to follow your classroom management plan as it's written. Stay true to your promises and high-bar standards.
